prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six openings placed B001 first, which I treat as a convergence of independent judgements and not as proof of merit. On merit the case is strong. The arc runs from proglucagon processing and the identification of the truncated active peptide GLP-1(7-36) amide, through human incretin physiology, to receptor-based therapies with large randomized outcome trials in type 2 diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal disease. The mechanism is original and clear, the clinical scale is very large, and it has two decades of independent confirmation, so the work is mature. A discovery-centred trio of Holst (human physiology and secretion), Drucker (GLP-1 and GLP-2 biology, receptor pathway and translation) and Mojsov (identification and synthesis of the bioactive peptide) credits the scientific discovery rather than the product.
statement.case_against: Attribution is the real weakness. The three-person limit forces us to leave out Lotte Bjerre Knudsen, whose long-acting acylated analogues are what actually reached patients, and perhaps Joel Habener, whose group worked on the same peptide and whose absence from the credited names is awkward given the priority questions around Mojsov. A prize built on the physiology arm may look detached from the drugs that justify it, while one that includes the drug arm drops a discoverer. I also worry that Mojsov's role is contested and that I am relying on general knowledge of that dispute. The committee must be able to defend whichever trio it picks.

responses.point: Perlmann ranked B001 first but placed the unfolded protein response (B051, Walter and Mori) third, ahead of CAR-T, as a conceptually clean ER-to-nucleus signalling discovery that is textbook after three decades.
responses.response: I agree that B051 is a clean two-person attribution, and that its maturity is a plus. I rank it below the clinical candidates because its therapeutic and disease-level consequences are still being worked out, while the Nobel criterion of benefit to humankind is already met by B001, B004 and B017. Its clean attribution makes it a strong future or paired candidate. I would not put it ahead of the engineered-T-cell field at this stage, and I do not see it as a rival to B001.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranked TNF blockade (B010, Feldmann and Maini) second as a clean and fully mature pair, and put the B- and T-lymphocyte lineage work (B008, Miller and Cooper) fourth, citing the age of both candidates as an argument for acting soon.
responses.response: The Feldmann-Maini attribution is cleaner than most of what we have, and I ranked B010 fifth on its merits. I would qualify two points. First, TNF blockade is one of several cytokine-targeting successes, including IL-6, so the case for it is a stronger one if we are willing to honour that class by a single exemplar. Second, I do not think advanced age should decide between B008 and clinical-impact candidates. Miller and Cooper are foundational, but that argument counts only if the committee accepts a purely conceptual immunology prize this year, and I am not yet persuaded it should come before a therapy that is changing care now.

responses.point: Sandberg proposed a two-person CAR-T credit (June and Sadelain), leaving out Rosenberg because his case fits adoptive T-cell transfer better, and ranked cGAS-STING (B050) fourth with Chen and Barber as the natural pair.
responses.response: I think the two-person CAR-T split is a fair reading of who designed and validated clinically effective CARs, and it keeps the credit near the real invention, but I would not exclude Rosenberg lightly because his adoptive transfer and early engineered-T-cell trials are part of the lineage. I disagree on B050 only in timing. The cGAS-STING mechanism is crisp, but with no established clinical impact I would not put it ahead of B004 or B017 this year.

responses.point: El-Manira ranked optogenetics (B012) second as a transformative method for experimental physiology, and acknowledged that six credited names exceed the limit so any trio excludes deserving people.
responses.response: I share the view that optogenetics is Nobel-scale, and I ranked it second myself. As a neurologist I am also aware that it has not yet changed patient care. My reservation is attribution: Nagel and Hegemann (channelrhodopsin), Deisseroth and Boyden (neuronal use) and Bamberg and Miesenböck cannot be cut to three without a defensible principle. Choosing the channel discoverers plus one implementer is arguable, but Boyden's and Bamberg's claims are strong enough that I would hold B012 as a prize for a later year unless the committee can agree a rule for the cut.

uncertainties: Whether to credit Mojsov, and how to treat Joel Habener, given the priority dispute over the active GLP-1 peptide; I rely on general knowledge and have not verified this.
Whether Knudsen should replace one of the discovery-side laureates to tie the prize to the approved drugs.
Whether a discovery-centred B001 trio is stronger than a two-part prize pairing GLP-1 with a second distinct achievement, given the three-person limit.
Order among B017, B004 and B012 if B001 is set aside or shares the prize.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile for the shortlisted candidates. I overlap with Thomas Perlmann as a frequent co-author on dopamine-neuron work and I trained with Paul Greengard, but neither is connected to any shortlisted candidate. I am not aware of a personal tie to any credited name.
